models.collectorNote: Regularly trades in the $3M-plus range in recent years. Provenance and service history matter more than mileage, deferred turbo and belt maintenance is expensive and common.

generations.name: Production run
generations.note: US-spec cars made 471 hp; European cars were rated at 478 PS and skipped the catalytic converters early on. Lexan windows and pull-cord doors on most cars, weight was the whole brief.

models.intro: Enzo Ferrari's last signed-off car, built for the company's 40th anniversary. A twin-turbo V8, a Kevlar-and-carbon body, no ABS, no power steering, no apology. About 1,300 were built and it remains the rawest road car Ferrari has ever sold.
models.name: F40
models.photoCredit: Photo: TTTNIS, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

photos.caption: 1990 Ferrari F40 front
photos.credit: Photo: TTTNIS, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

models.collectorNote: Coupes have traded around $3M–$4M and Apertas well above that. Hybrid battery health is the big ownership question as these cars age.

generations.name: Coupe
generations.note: The V12 alone makes 789 hp; the HY-KERS motor fills the torque gaps rather than driving the car on electricity. 0–60 mph in under three seconds, in a car with no electric-only mode worth mentioning.

generations.name: Aperta
generations.note: Open-top version with a removable carbon roof and revised aero to cope without a fixed roof. Same powertrain, higher price, even smaller production run.

models.intro: Ferrari's hybrid flagship and its answer to the McLaren P1 and Porsche 918. A 6.3-litre V12 plus a KERS electric motor, 499 coupes, then 210 Aperta roadsters. Offered by invitation only, and most never left collections.
models.name: LaFerrari
models.photoCredit: Photo: Calreyn88, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

photos.caption: 2014 Laferrari 4
photos.credit: Photo: Calreyn88, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

models.collectorNote: Values climbed hard in the 2010s, then settled. The F512 M is the rare one; the 512 TR is arguably the best to drive. Budget for engine-out belt services.

generations.name: Original Testarossa
generations.note: Early cars had a single high-mounted mirror, the 'monospecchio', and knock-off wheels. US cars were detuned slightly versus European spec.

generations.name: 512 TR
generations.note: A serious rework, not a facelift: more power, a revised chassis, better weight distribution and a cleaner nose without the pop-ups' worst habits.

generations.name: F512 M
generations.note: The final evolution: fixed headlights, round tail lights and the most power of the run. Only 501 built, and the most collectible of the three.

models.intro: The poster car of the 1980s. Side strakes feeding side-mounted radiators, a flat-12 mounted low in the middle, and a starring role on Miami Vice. Nearly 10,000 were built across the Testarossa, 512 TR and F512 M, huge numbers for a Ferrari flagship.
models.name: Testarossa
models.photoCredit: Photo: Mr.choppers, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

photos.caption: 1986 Ferrari Testarossa being unloaded
photos.credit: Photo: Mr.choppers, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

models.collectorNote: Low-mile examples have traded above $3M–$4M at auction. The F1 gearbox and clutch wear make a pre-purchase inspection by a Ferrari specialist non-negotiable.

generations.name: Production run
generations.note: The 6.0-litre Tipo F140 V12 revved to 8,200 rpm and became the basis for the FXX track car and the Maserati MC12. No manual was ever offered, the paddles were the point.

models.intro: Named for the founder and built as a Formula 1 car in road clothes, carbon tub, automated-manual gearbox, carbon-ceramic brakes, and aero that generated serious downforce without a big rear wing. 400 built, including the last one for the Pope.
models.name: Enzo
models.photoCredit: Photo: TTTNIS, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

photos.caption: 2004 Enzo Ferrari rear
photos.credit: Photo: TTTNIS, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

generations.name: First generation
generations.note: Shares its platform and much of its hardware with the Portofino but wears a completely different body. The Spider replaced the retractable hardtop with a fabric roof.

models.intro: Ferrari's front-engined coupé in its softest suit: clean, retro-leaning styling, a 2+ cabin and the twin-turbo V8 from the Portofino turned up. The Spider convertible followed. It's the Ferrari for people who found the rest of the range too shouty.
models.name: Roma
models.photoCredit: Photo: Calreyn88, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

photos.caption: 2021 Ferrari Roma 6
photos.credit: Photo: Calreyn88, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

models.collectorNote: Chassis 3413 GT made $48,405,000 at RM Sotheby's Monterey in 2018, then the world auction record for a car. A 1963 car was reported sold privately the same year at around $70 million, a figure never confirmed by buyer or seller. Provenance is everything here.

generations.name: 250 GTO (Series I)
generations.note: Thirty-six cars, each hand-finished and slightly different. The 3.0 litre Colombo V12 made 300 hp through a gated five-speed. GTOs won the International Championship for GT Manufacturers in 1962, 1963 and 1964, and beat Cobras and E-types doing it.

generations.name: 250 GTO Series II (GTO/64)
generations.note: For 1964 Scaglietti gave a handful of cars a wider, lower body with a roof spoiler and a reshaped nose. The mechanical package carried over. Series II cars closed out the model's run at the front of GT racing before the mid-engined era arrived.

models.intro: The most valuable production car line in the world began as a homologation argument. Ferrari needed a GT racer for 1962, built 36 cars around the Colombo V12, and persuaded the FIA the GTO was a version of the 250 SWB. It then won the manufacturers' title three years straight.
